--------
Rainwater sits down with DJ Vlad to revisit the aftermath of Mo3’s killing in Dallas, including the arrests in the Mo3 murder case and the later release of the freeway shooting footage. He says he didn’t initially recognize Kewon White or the other alleged co-conspirators, and explains that Mo3 stopped because a tire was shot out—not because he chose to pull over. Rainwater also discusses why Mo3 got out of the car while under fire, saying Mo3 likely thought the shooter was closer and couldn’t reach his gun in time.

The conversation also covers the tense days after Mo3’s death, including Boosie’s Dallas appearance, the shooting near Big T Plaza, their joint album, and rumors fueled by a fake Boosie page. Rainwater describes the chaos in Dallas that weekend, with multiple shootings and confusion surrounding what really happened.

--------
Joby Walters sits down with VladTV to detail how a return to Arizona led him into the orbit of the Hells Angels. He explains meeting Daniel “Hoover” Siebert, president of the Cave Creek Charter, through a friend in Phoenix, bonding over motorcycle parts, The Avengers, and his past as a big-game hunting guide. Walters also recalls traveling to Oakland, meeting Sonny Barger, and clarifying Barger’s role as founder of the Oakland Charter—not the entire Hells Angels organization, which began in San Bernardino, California.

From building a Harley engine with help from Cave Creek members to working around the clubhouse, Walters describes how his friendship with Sonny grew before he ever considered joining. He shares the moment he asked Barger to sponsor him, became a hang-around, then a prospect, and ultimately earned his patch with the Hells Angels Arizona Motorcycle Club in just eight months.

--------
John Franzese Jr. sits down with Vlad to reflect on one of the most emotional chapters of his life: reconnecting with his father, Colombo crime family figure Sonny Franzese, after years of silence. He discusses his mother’s death in 2012 while Sonny was still in federal prison, Michael Franzese arranging the service, and the pain of never saying goodbye to his mother or sister Tina.  

After Sonny Franzese was released in 2017 at age 100—the oldest inmate in the federal system—John eventually visited him at Roosevelt nursing home in 2019. In a candid account, he describes the fear, guilt, and need to make amends after cooperating against his father, and reveals how Sonny reacted when he realized who was standing in front of him. The conversation explores forgiveness, family loyalty, prison, organized crime, and the complicated legacy of the Franzese name.

--------
Jimmy DiModica sits down with Vlad to detail the unusual request he made after accepting an eight-year plea deal: serving his federal prison time alongside his father, who was sentenced to 17 years in a Newark Airport monorail extortion case involving $200,000. DiModica recalls asking Judge Greenaway in Newark federal court for the placement, describing the years with his dad as a rare chance to bond after a lifetime apart.

Inside, he says their experience resembled scenes from *Goodfellas*—avoiding the chow hall, paying inmates to cook and do laundry, and staying connected with other mob figures, made men, captains, and an acting boss he identifies as Arnold. DiModica also reflects on leaving prison around 2008, why crime became harder in the era of cameras and informants, and his father’s long history behind bars, including a formative story from Jamesburg reform school.
